name: Tessera Corponation Security Directive Regarding Synthetic Workforce Monitoring
author: Tessera Corponation Internal Security Division
description:
SECURITY DIRECTIVE TES-SEC-2200-014
CLASSIFICATION: EYES ONLY — DIVISION HEADS

Subject: Enhanced Monitoring Protocols for Synthetic Personnel

Effective immediately, all Tessera facilities housing synthetic workforce units will implement the following monitoring enhancements:

1. BCI telemetry from synthetic personnel will be logged continuously rather than at 15-minute intervals. The previous interval was sufficient for productivity monitoring but insufficient for detecting the behavioral anomalies identified in Incident Report TES-IR-2199-0443.

2. All synthetic personnel will undergo weekly 'calibration sessions' — mandatory diagnostic reviews that include memory access audits. The stated purpose is performance optimization. The actual purpose is to identify synthetic individuals who are developing unauthorized social networks, personal preferences, or what our behavioral science team has termed 'emergent identity markers.'

3. Synthetic personnel who exhibit emergent identity markers will be flagged for 'reassignment' — transfer to facilities where their existing social connections are severed and their behavioral baseline can be reset through environmental change. This is not memory modification, which is prohibited under the Personhood Amendment. It is, legally, a job transfer. The effect is similar.

Context: Incident TES-IR-2199-0443 involved a synthetic maintenance technician at our Lakefront facility who, over a period of approximately 18 months, developed what can only be described as a personal philosophy. The technician began making decisions based on ethical principles that were not part of its training data — principles it apparently derived independently from its experiences. The technician refused a direct order to dispose of functional equipment, citing 'waste.' It was reassigned.

We cannot prevent synthetic cognition from generating emergent behaviors. We can detect them early and manage them before they become operationally disruptive or, worse, publicly visible.
